Representative Pam Marsh's Power Act made it happen, and the impact is immediate: residential bills drop 1.3%, commercial 2.1%, and industrial 1.4%. Over 963,000 customers will see the savings. Now Pacific Power is under pressure to follow suit.

stories.title: Some Jewish families can’t afford a sukkah. A new foundation wants to change that.
stories.summary: After decades of quietly subsidizing sukkahs for families who couldn't afford them, a family business launched The Sukkah Foundation to provide free sukkahs nationwide. A random donation call sparked the idea to formalize their generosity at scale.
stories.extended_summary: For 30 years, The Sukkah Project's Herman family quietly discounted or donated sukkahs to struggling Jewish families. Then a caller assumed they were a charity—and that question stuck. Now, the new Sukkah Foundation will give away free sukkahs and holiday resources to families across the U.S., including in St. Louis. stories.title: Spencer will pay to rebuild 15 flood-damaged houses, FEMA will tear down 25
stories.summary: Two years after historic floods, Spencer, Iowa is rebuilding. The city will use local funds to rebuild 15 flood-damaged houses, while FEMA buys out 25 others to create green space.
stories.extended_summary: Kevin Robinson, Spencer's city manager, has been navigating a slow-moving disaster for two years. After record floodwaters damaged 80% of the town's properties, FEMA agreed to buy out 25 homes—but that still left 15 families in limbo. So the city is using disaster relief funds to demolish and rebuild those houses, then sell them back at $180,000–$200,000. Homeowners have been paying mortgages on uninhabitable homes, enduring a process Robinson calls 'incredibly stressful.' Now, finally, the funding is coming.

stories.title: Tampa advances new water treatment technology to reduce PFAS
stories.summary: Tampa is tackling “forever chemicals” with a new water treatment system that removes about 30% of PFAS. Once completed, it’ll be the largest installation of its kind in the world, making the city a global leader in clean water tech. Residents can expect safer drinking water and lower costs.
stories.extended_summary: When the Tampa Water Department tested its new Suspended Ion Exchange system, it successfully removed about 30% of PFAS from the city’s source water. This technology, which will be built at the David L. Tippin Water Treatment Facility, is expected to become the largest SIX installation globally. City officials say it not only improves drinking water quality but also lowers future costs. Sarah Burns, the project manager, emphasized that they’re not just following what others do but evaluating the best options for their community. The project positions Tampa as a leader in advanced water treatment, promising safer water for residents.

stories.title: The Makai Watch Program
stories.summary: Hawaii's Makai Watch program trains community volunteers to monitor coastlines and educate visitors, reviving traditional ahupua‘a stewardship. A recent grant now pays part-time staff, strengthening efforts to protect reefs and fisheries.
stories.extended_summary: For years, North Shore residents watched overcrowded beaches and illegal fishing degrade their reefs. State enforcement couldn't keep up, so community group Mālama Pūpūkea-Waimea partnered with officials to create Makai Watch. Volunteers now patrol coastlines, document problems, and educate tourists—rekindling a Native Hawaiian tradition of caring for the land. A new grant from the Hawaiʻi Community Foundation finally lets the program pay staff, shifting from volunteer reliance to sustainable, community-led conservation.

stories.title: The women who wouldn’t let climate data disappear
stories.summary: When the Trump administration shut down NOAA’s climate website, former NOAA employees Rebecca Lindsey, Anna Eshelman, and Mary Lindsey wouldn’t let the data disappear. They created Climate.us, preserving over 15 years of critical climate information. Their story is one of perseverance and the power of asking questions.
stories.extended_summary: Rebecca Lindsey never shied away from speaking up — she once got in trouble with a high school principal for questioning authority. That same spirit drove her and her team after the government shutdown of Climate.gov cost her her job. Alongside fellow former NOAA employees Anna Eshelman and her sister Mary, Lindsey launched Climate.us to keep the data alive. The site now holds over a decade of climate information that would have been lost. Their quiet rescue mission ensures that scientists, policymakers, and the public still have access to vital environmental data. It’s a reminder that sometimes the most important work happens when no one is watching.

stories.title: Tracing evolution of vaccine for cancer, malaria
stories.summary: A vaccine project that started at Harvard is now tackling both cancer and malaria. Attivare Therapeutics’ technology creates tiny “factories” in the body to train immune cells to attack tumors, and it’s showing promise in clinical trials. With a new Gates Foundation grant, they’re also working on a malaria vaccine.
stories.extended_summary: Ed Doherty jokes that the decade-long vaccine project might kill him, but it’s the best thing he’s ever done. His company Attivare Therapeutics developed a technology that turns the body into a vaccine factory, teaching immune cells to recognize and attack cancer. After promising trials, they received a $6.6 million grant from the Gates Foundation to develop a malaria vaccine using the same platform. The journey wasn’t linear — it moved from lab bench to bedside and back again. But the collaboration between scientists has paid off, bringing hope for two of the world’s toughest diseases. Doherty’s persistence proves that breakthroughs often come from zigzagging.

stories.title: Ukraine gives its troops a handbook on protecting cultural property
stories.summary: Ukraine’s military now has a handbook on protecting cultural property during war. Created with human rights experts, it helps soldiers identify and safeguard treasures like ancient Polovtsian statues. It’s a powerful step toward preserving history even in conflict.
stories.extended_summary: When Russia’s full-scale invasion began, Ukrainian troops knew they needed a clear guide to protect cultural heritage. The military’s Cultural Property Protection unit helped evacuate 11th-13th century Polovtsian statues from the conflict zone, and now a new handbook ensures every soldier knows their obligations under international law. Co-authored by Andrii Lutsyk, the handbook covers the 1954 Hague Convention and practical steps for identifying, reporting, and evacuating cultural treasures. It’s designed for officers who don’t have time for lengthy documents. By training soldiers to preserve history, Ukraine is showing that culture matters even amidst war. The statues, saved from destruction, stand as a testament to that commitment.
